segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: though in fact Jesus himself was not baptizing; his disciples were—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he left Judea and went away again to Galilee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he had to pass through Samaria.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of land that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jacob’s spring was there. So Jesus, tired out from the journey, sat down just as he was beside the spring. It was about the sixth hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Give me a drink.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For his disciples had gone away into the town to buy food.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Samaritan woman said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The woman said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, you have no bucket, and the well is deep. Where then do you get this living water?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Surely you are not greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but whoever drinks the water that I will give them will never be thirsty again. Instead, the water that I will give them will become in them a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The woman said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or keep coming all the way here to draw.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go, call your husband, and come back here.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The woman answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I have no husband.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are right to say, ‘I have no husband,’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: for you have had five husbands, and the man you have now is not your husband. In this you have spoken the truth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The woman said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, I see that you are a prophet.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you people say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Believe me, woman, an hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But an hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking just such people to worship him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The woman said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I know that Messiah is coming,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the one called Christ.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “When he comes, he will tell us everything.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I am he, the one speaking to you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just then his disciples came, and they were amazed that he was speaking with a woman. Yet no one said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you want?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: or,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why are you speaking with her?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the woman left her water jar and went away into the town and said to the people,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did! Could this be the Messiah?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went out of the town and were coming to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Meanwhile the disciples were urging him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, eat.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I have food to eat that you do not know about.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the disciples said to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Surely no one has brought him something to eat?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “My food is to do the will of the one who sent me and to complete his work.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do you not say, ‘Four months more, and then the harvest comes’? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes and see the fields: they are white for harvest. Already

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: the reaper is receiving wages and gathering a crop for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For in this the saying is true: ‘One sows and another reaps.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I sent you to reap what you have not labored for. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He told me everything I did.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And many more believed because of his word,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they said to the woman,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We no longer believe because of what you said, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After the two days he left there for Galilee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen everything he had done in Jerusalem at the festival, for they too had gone to the festival.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. Now there was a certain royal official whose son was sick in Capernaum.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and begged him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will never believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The official said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, come down before my child dies.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go; your son lives.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was already on his way down when his slaves met him and told him that his boy was alive.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they told him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the father realized that it was at that very hour that Jesus had said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Your son lives.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he believed, he and his whole household.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This was now the second sign that Jesus performed after coming from Judea to Galilee.

notes.note: The narrator and Jesus use the word for a spring or source (here and in verse 14), while the woman uses a different word meaning a dug well (verses 11–12). Most translations say “well” throughout. Keeping the two words apart lets the reader hear the link between Jacob’s spring and the “spring of water welling up” that Jesus promises.

Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon, the hottest part of the day; the seventh hour in verse 52 is about one in the afternoon. A minority of scholars think John counts from midnight, but most do not accept this.

The verb can mean to associate on friendly terms or, more narrowly, to use something together with someone. On the second reading the point is that Jews would not share a drinking vessel with Samaritans for reasons of purity, which fits the scene well. The sentence is the narrator’s explanation, and a few early manuscripts lack it.

In ordinary usage, including the Greek Old Testament, “living water” meant fresh, flowing water from a spring or stream as opposed to still water in a cistern. The woman takes Jesus in this everyday sense, which is why she asks where he will get it without a bucket. Jesus means water that gives life.

The adjective is formed from the word for “age,” and in Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come. It describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. “Eternal” is the standard rendering and is kept here; a minority of translators prefer “life of the age to come.”

The mountain is Gerizim, which rises above the site and was the holy place of the Samaritans. Their temple there had been destroyed by the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus in the late second century BC, but they continued to worship on the mountain. Where God was to be worshiped was the central dispute between Samaritans and Jews.

Greek manuscripts did not distinguish capital letters, so “spirit” here may be the human spirit, meaning inward and genuine worship, or God’s Spirit, meaning worship made possible by the Spirit whom Jesus gives. Many interpreters of John favor the second, given how the Gospel speaks of the Spirit elsewhere. The lower-case rendering leaves the question open.

“Messiah” here is a Greek spelling of the Hebrew and Aramaic word for “anointed one,” and “Christ” is its Greek translation. The explanation is probably the narrator’s aside for Greek readers, as at 1:41, though it could be read as part of the woman’s speech. Samaritans did not use the title Messiah, as far as is known, but expected a prophet like Moses who would restore and reveal all things.

notes.traditional: I that speak unto thee am he
notes.note: The Greek is literally “I am, the one speaking to you.” In context it is the ordinary way of saying “I am he,” that is, the Messiah she has just mentioned. Many scholars also hear in it the first of John’s absolute “I am” sayings, which echo God’s self-declarations in Isaiah.

The Greek word is the one translated “Christ” in verse 25. Here it is a title under discussion, not a name, and a first-century hearer would have heard the role of the expected anointed deliverer, which “Messiah” conveys to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels. The form of the woman’s question in Greek is tentative, neither a confident claim nor a denial.

The word “already” stands at the boundary between two sentences and can go with either. Older translations attach it to what precedes: the fields are “already white for harvest.” The Greek edition followed here, with many modern translations, takes it with what follows: the reaper is already receiving wages.

The word can mean a homeland or a hometown, and it is disputed which place John means. If it is Galilee, the welcome in verse 45 is shallow, resting only on the signs people had seen. If it is Judea or Jerusalem, the saying explains why Jesus left there. Interpreters remain divided.

The word means someone attached to a king, whether a courtier, an officer, or a member of the royal household. In Galilee this would be a man in the service of Herod Antipas, the ruler of the region, who was popularly called king. Whether the man was Jewish or a Gentile is not stated.

The Greek word denotes people owned by a master, not hired staff. “Servants” is the traditional English rendering, but it suggests free employees to a modern reader. Slaves in a wealthy household could hold responsible positions, yet they remained their master’s property.

candidates.reason: Translations split between “servant” and “slave” across the Gospels, parables and Paul’s self-descriptions, and readers will be misled if the English varies without a rule.
The vocative ranges from polite “Sir” to “Lord” as a confession, and a consistent policy is needed for when the address to Jesus shifts from one to the other.
The verb covers both cultic worship and bowing down in homage before a person, so “worship” versus “bow down before” needs one rule, especially where people do it to Jesus.
Capitalization (Spirit or spirit) and the choice among spirit, wind and breath recur throughout the New Testament and need a single policy.
Older versions vary between “sign” and “miracle,” and John’s numbered signs depend on the same English word being used throughout.
